rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-4 - the authors report their own prototype sensor readings taken on 2 May 2024 (temperature 22.1-28 C, humidity 39-49.1 %, soil moisture 62.5-65 %, water level 60-62 %) from an ESP32-based IoT irrigation controller.
rows.notes: The study builds and demonstrates an ESP32/IoT smart irrigation controller with in-field contact sensors (DHT22, soil moisture probe, ultrasonic water level) and a web dashboard; it involves no remote sensing (satellite, aerial or drone imagery). It also reports no measured water savings, only monitoring data and assertions of improved efficiency.

rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-4 - own prototype sensor readings over one day (2 May 2024) from an ESP32-based IoT irrigation system transmitted via Server-Sent Events to a web/mobile dashboard.
rows.notes: The technology (IoT smart sensors with threshold-based pump control and a web interface) matches the claim, but the study reports only real-time monitoring data (temperature, humidity, soil moisture, water level) over a single day in a 'realistic simulation of agricultural conditions'. No water consumption, irrigation volumes, or comparison with conventional irrigation are measured; the statements about improved irrigation efficiency and water savings are assertions, not results. The study therefore supports only a precondition (monitoring/control capability) of the claimed water-conservation effect. The authors do list limitations (connectivity, sensor reliability, energy, prototype scale, farmer adoption) but these apply to the system, not to any measured water-conservation result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-4 - own sensor readings on 2 May 2024 (T 22.1-28 C, RH 39-49.1 %, soil moisture 62.5-65 %, water level 60-62 %), the same values quoted in the review passage.
rows.notes: The ranges quoted in the passage are the study's own monitoring readings, so the study does validate real-time monitoring of those variables. However, it does not report any result on water consumption reduction: no water-use measurement, no control comparison, no yield data. The 38 % soil-moisture pump threshold is described as determined after 'extensive testing' but no test data are shown. The claimed 'consumption reduction under real operational conditions' is an assertion in the discussion/abstract, and the authors themselves call the setup a prototype in a realistic simulation. Only the precondition (monitoring/digital control capability) is supported.
